sections.title: How does the Square of a binomial calculator work?
sections.html:
The Square of a binomial calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports insert the result (Simple binomial expansion) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (choose the calculation that you would like to perform); then you type in the insert your · b (Expansion of (ax ± b)2 given a and b), the atimes 2, the b pos and the subt binomial hide.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Square of a binomial calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Insert the result=(insert your · a ^ 2) + 2 × insert your · a × insert your · b + (insert your · b ^ 2)
Insert your · a=insert your · b + the square root of (insert the result)
Insert your · a=(1 ÷ 2) × atimes 2
Atimes 2 pos=-atimes 2
Insert your · a=the square root of (a sq)
Insert your · b=-b pos

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Square of a binomial calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the insert your · b (Expansion of (ax ± b)2 given a and b), the atimes 2 and the b pos — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Square of a binomial calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns insert the result (Simple binomial expansion), derived from the insert your · b (Expansion of (ax ± b)2 given a and b), the atimes 2 and the b pos. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Square of a binomial calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the insert your · b (Expansion of (ax ± b)2 given a and b), the atimes 2 and the b pos, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Insert the result = 400. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Square of a binomial calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
